summary: Describes the canonical form of an XML document, a standard way of writing it so allowed differences such as spacing do not matter. This helps when comparing or signing XML. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Two people can write the same sentence with different spacing. This defines one neat way to write it so they match exactly.

subtitle: A standard way to write an XML document so that harmless differences in formatting disappear.

tldr.problem: XML 1.0 and Namespaces in XML let the same information be written in many ways, such as different attribute order, entity use or encoding, which makes it hard to tell whether a document has really changed.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines a canonical form built from the XPath data model: UTF-8 output, resolved references, no XML declaration or DTD, sorted namespace declarations and attributes, double-quoted values and expanded empty elements.
tldr.outcome: Documents with the same canonical form are logically equivalent, apart from a few unusual cases, which makes canonical form useful for digital signatures. The reverse is not guaranteed.

today: RFC 3076 is an Informational memo and the metadata lists no replacement or update. Its own text anticipates that a future version could address its limitations.

sections.title: Why Canonical XML
sections.content:
Documents that are equivalent for many applications can still differ in physical representation: their entity structure, attribute order and character encoding can all vary. This specification defines a method for producing a canonical form that accounts for the changes XML 1.0 and Namespaces permit.

The main use is testing whether the information content of a document has changed. A digital signature, for instance, can be computed over the canonical form, so the signing and relying parties get the same digest provided the document differs only in logically equivalent ways.
sections.eli5: If everyone writes a message in the same neat style first, you can tell at once whether anyone changed the words.

sections.title: What Canonicalization Changes
sections.content:
The memo summarizes the changes:

  • The document is encoded in UTF-8 and line breaks are normalized to #xA.
  • Attribute values are normalized, character and parsed entity references are replaced, and CDATA sections become plain character content.
  • The XML declaration and document type declaration are removed.
  • Empty elements become start-end tag pairs, and attribute values use double quotes.
  • Superfluous namespace declarations are removed and default attributes are added.
  • Namespace declarations and attributes of each element are put in lexicographic order.

All whitespace inside the document element is kept, while whitespace outside it is discarded.
sections.eli5: It tidies the document: same quote marks, same ordering, no extras, so two tidy copies look identical.

sections.title: The Data Model and Ordering
sections.content:
Canonicalization is defined on the XPath 1.0 data model, using a node-set. Input is either an octet stream containing a well-formed XML document, which implementations MUST support, or a node-set for document subsets, which they SHOULD support. A second parameter says whether comments are included. Implementations MUST be able to produce output without comments, and support for canonical XML with comments is RECOMMENDED.

For ordering, namespace nodes come before attribute nodes. Namespace nodes are sorted by local name, with the default namespace first. Attributes are sorted with namespace URI as the primary key and local name as the secondary key. Implementations MUST report failure on documents containing relative namespace URIs.
sections.eli5: Think of a list of everything in the document. The rules say in which order to write each thing down so the result is always the same.

sections.title: Processing and Document Subsets
sections.content:
Nodes are written in document order and the result is encoded in UTF-8 without a byte order mark. Attribute values and text are escaped differently: in attributes, &, < and the double quote become character references, and tab, line feed and carriage return become 	, 
 and ; in text, &, <, > and carriage return are replaced.

For a document subset, attributes in the xml namespace such as xml:lang and xml:space are inherited from omitted ancestors. The canonical form of a whole document is well-formed, and applying the method again to well-formed canonical output changes nothing.
sections.eli5: Special characters get written in a fixed code, so a tricky character always looks the same.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
Section 3 of the memo gives seven examples. They show the loss of the XML declaration and DTD, retention of whitespace in content, empty elements becoming tag pairs, namespace and attribute sorting, character reference replacement, entity replacement, transcoding to UTF-8, and canonicalizing a document subset.

One example shows <e3 name = "elem3" id="elem3" /> becoming <e3 id="elem3" name="elem3"></e3>, with attributes sorted and the empty element expanded.
sections.eli5: The memo shows messy documents next to their tidy versions so you can see the rules at work.

sections.title: Limits and Design Decisions
sections.content:
The memo is explicit that equal canonical forms imply equivalence, with limits, but different canonical forms do not prove a difference, because application-specific rules such as black versus rgb(0,0,0) are out of scope. Loss of the base URI, of notations and unparsed entities, and of attribute types in the DTD can make a canonical form not fully operational.

It also records choices: no XML declaration, no Unicode character model normalization beyond requiring Normalization Form C when converting from non-UCS encodings, and no namespace prefix rewriting. Rewriting was dropped because prefixes can carry meaning, for example inside an XPath expression in an attribute value.
sections.eli5: Tidying cannot catch every kind of sameness, and the authors chose not to rename things in ways that could break meaning.

viz.caption: INPUT AND CANONICAL FORM FROM THE RFC (SECTION 3.3, ONE ELEMENT)

data.title: Attribute sorting and empty element
data.code:
Input:      <e3    name = "elem3"   id="elem3"    />
Canonical:  <e3 id="elem3" name="elem3"></e3>
